screens.title: EC2 Advanced Topics: Storage, Scaling, and Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will connect three practical concerns every developer faces in production: durable block storage, automatic compute scaling, and traffic distribution. You will learn how Amazon EBS provides persistent, network-attached block volumes and when to choose SSD or HDD types. We will then build on that storage foundation to explore Auto Scaling Groups, which automatically adjust EC2 capacity using launch templates and scaling policies. Finally, you will see how Elastic Load Balancers route traffic to targets and perform health checks so your application remains available across Availability Zones. Along the way I’ll give concrete examples, like creating a launch template with user data to install Nginx, configuring an Application Load Balancer to route HTTP traffic, and using a target tracking policy to maintain average C P U utilization. We’ll also highlight common pitfalls, such as relying on ephemeral instance store volumes for critical data or forgetting health checks. By the end, you’ll understand the developer implications of integrating EBS, ASG, and ELB and be able to design a highly available, cost-aware architecture that supports CI/CD deployments.

EC2 Advanced Topics
Storage, scaling, and load balancing to make applications resilient and cost-effective.
In this presentation you will see how EBS volumes provide persistent block storage, how Auto Scaling Groups adjust capacity with launch templates and scaling policies, and how Elastic Load Balancers route traffic and run health checks. Each piece plays a role in availability, performance, and developer workflow.

Coming up

Concept preview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
ALB → Target Group
ASG (Launch Template)
EBS: gp3 / io2 / st1

Correctly choosing storage and automating scaling and routing reduces downtime, controls cost, and simplifies developer deployments.

Each objective is both conceptual and practical: you will differentiate gp3, io2, st1 and sc1 in terms of IOPS and throughput, and you will understand when snapshots are the right recovery mechanism. You will practice creating a launch template that embeds a user data script to bootstrap instances and then link that template to an ASG. These skills matter because they let you build applications that tolerate failures, handle variable load, and minimize manual intervention. To verify competency you will be able to explain why ephemeral instance store volumes are unsuitable for critical data and demonstrate a working ALB + ASG connection using a launch template.

screens.title: Amazon EBS: persistent block storage
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Elastic Block Store provides persistent block-level storage for EC2 instances. Unlike ephemeral instance store, which is tied to the lifecycle of a single instance and disappears on stop or termination, EBS volumes persist independently. They are network-attached within an Availability Zone and can be detached from one instance and attached to another in the same AZ. This makes EBS suitable for data that must survive instance replacement, such as databases and user data directories. A common example is attaching an EBS volume as a boot volume or separate data volume for a database; if the instance fails, the volume remains and can be reattached after launching a replacement. A frequent misconception is treating EBS as remote object storage: EBS behaves like a block device to the OS, not an object store; snapshots are stored in S3 but an EBS volume itself is presented as a disk. Key operational tips: ensure your data is on EBS for critical state, take snapshots regularly to protect against accidental deletion, and remember EBS volumes are zonal — to move data across regions you must snapshot and copy. When designing for high availability, combine EBS with AMIs and automation so new instances can reattach volumes or restore from snapshots without manual steps. What will you preserve in EBS versus rebuild from code and configuration?

keyIdea.text: EBS provides durable, network-attached block storage that persists independently of instance lifecycle and must be managed with snapshots for recovery.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › EBS: persistent block storage
What EBS provides
  • Persistent block device presented to EC2 that survives instance termination if not deleted.
  • Detachable within the same Availability Zone so volumes can be moved between instances.
  • Used for boot volumes, databases, and any data requiring durability beyond instance lifetime.
Analogy
Think of an EBS volume as a portable hard disk in a data center rack: it plugs into a server and remains when the server is replaced.
Concrete example
A database runs on an EC2 instance with its data directory on an attached EBS volume. If the instance fails, an operator can launch a replacement instance, attach the EBS volume, and the database starts with the same data.
Common mistake
Using instance store for critical persistent data — you lose data when the instance is stopped or terminated.
Key Takeaway
Use EBS for any data you must retain across instance lifecycle and snapshot regularly for recovery and cross-zone copying.

screens.title: EBS Volume Types and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: EBS offers several volume types optimized for different input and output profiles. General purpose SSDs, gp2 and gp3, provide a balance of cost and performance and are excellent for boot volumes and development environments. For transactional systems that need high and consistent IOPS, io1 and io2 (Block Express variants) let you provision IOPS separately from size, making them ideal for databases and latency-sensitive workloads. For throughput-oriented tasks, such as big data processing, ETL, or log aggregation, st1 (throughput-optimized HDD) offers cost-effective sequential throughput. sc1 is a cold HDD for infrequent access to large datasets. A concrete decision example: a small web server uses gp3 for boot and app files; a relational database with heavy write activity uses io2 to meet latency and IOPS guarantees; an analytics cluster processing large sequential scans uses st1. A common misconception is assuming SSDs always outperform HDDs; for large sequential reads/writes where throughput matters more than IOPS, st1 can be far more cost-effective. When you plan capacity, document the workload input and output pattern, expected throughput, and cost constraints. Also consider snapshot frequency and restore time when selecting volume type, since the recovery plan affects availability and cost.

keyIdea.title: Choose by profile
keyIdea.text: Match EBS type to workload: gp3 for general, io2 for high IOPS, st1/sc1 for throughput and cold storage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › EBS Volume Types
Volume types
gp2 / gp3
General purpose SSD — boot volumes, apps
io1 / io2
Provisioned IOPS — transactional DBs
st1
Throughput HDD — big data / log processing
sc1
Cold HDD — infrequent large datasets
Decision checklist: identify read/write IOPS, sequential throughput needs, cost targets, and snapshot frequency before choosing a type.
Concrete scenario
A production database with high concurrent writes: choose io2 and provision IOPS to meet SLOs. A development server or small web tier: gp3 is cost-effective and easier to manage.
Misconception
SSD always best — not true when workload is sequential throughput-dominant where st1 can be cheaper and adequate.
Key Takeaway
Match volume to IOPS or throughput needs; document and test under load before committing.

screens.title: EBS Snapshots: backup and restore process
screens.narratorSegment: EBS snapshots create a point-in-time backup of a volume and are stored incrementally in Amazon S3. The typical process is straightforward: first, quiesce application writes if possible to ensure consistency; second, create a snapshot of the volume; third, snapshots store only changed blocks after the initial full snapshot, which saves storage and time. To recover, you create a new volume from a snapshot and attach it to an instance in the same Availability Zone, or copy the snapshot to another region then create a volume in that region. A concrete example: schedule nightly snapshots for a database volume; if an instance is accidentally terminated, create a new EC2 instance, create a volume from the latest snapshot, attach it, and start the database to restore state. Common misconceptions include treating snapshots as instantaneous full copies — the first snapshot captures all blocks but subsequent snapshots are incremental and the restore process reconstructs the full volume. Operational tips: automate snapshots via lifecycle policies, test restores regularly, and consider snapshot copy to another region for disaster recovery. How will you incorporate snapshot testing into your deployment pipeline?

keyIdea.text: EBS snapshots provide incremental, point-in-time backups stored in S3 and enable volume restore or cross-region copy for disaster recovery.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › EBS Snapshots
Snapshot steps
1. Quiesce writes
Flush DB buffers if possible
2. Create snapshot
Initial full snapshot then incremental
3. Restore when needed
Create volume from snapshot
Snapshots are stored incrementally in S3. After the first snapshot, only changed blocks are uploaded, which reduces storage and speeds subsequent backups. To move data between regions, copy the snapshot to the target region and then create volumes there.
Example scenario
Nightly snapshots for a database volume. When the primary fails, launch a replacement instance, create a volume from last snapshot, attach it, and start the DB to recover recent state.
Pro Tip
Automate snapshot lifecycle and test restores on a schedule to ensure backup integrity and recovery speed meet RTO/RPO targets.

screens.title: Launch Template and User Data Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: A launch template encapsulates the configuration an Auto Scaling Group uses to start EC2 instances: AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, and user data for bootstrapping. The user data script is executed on first boot and is an excellent place to install runtime dependencies. For example, the lesson’s sample bootstrap installs and starts Nginx and writes a simple H T M L file identifying the instance by hostname. Concrete example: a user data script that runs on Amazon Linux 2 will update packages, install Nginx, start the service, and create an index page using the instance hostname. Common mistakes include placing secrets directly in user data, which is visible to anyone who can describe the instance; instead use parameter stores or encrypted user data. Also avoid lengthy manual configuration in user data — prefer configuration management or immutable AMIs for repeatable builds. As a verification step, create the launch template, provision an ASG with two instances, and confirm each instance returns the expected H T M L page. How will you keep your bootstrap reproducible and secure across deployments?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Launch Template & User Data
Launch template components
  • AMI to use as the base image.
  • Instance type and EBS configuration.
  • Security groups and key pair for access.
  • User data script to bootstrap the instance at first boot.
Security note
Do not place secrets in user data. Use a secrets manager or instance profile to retrieve credentials securely.
Example user data
#!/bin/bash
yum update -y
yum install nginx -y
systemctl start nginx
systemctl enable nginx
echo "<h1>Hello from EC2 instance $(hostname -f)</h1>" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
This script installs Nginx, starts it, and writes a simple index page. In production, prefer baked AMIs or configuration management for large deployments.

screens.title: Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: An Auto Scaling Group manages a collection of EC2 instances and automatically adjusts capacity to meet defined requirements. It uses a launch template to create new instances with consistent configuration, and it enforces minimum, desired, and maximum capacity so you have predictable bounds on cost and availability. ASGs are typically integrated with CloudWatch metrics and scaling policies, allowing the group to trigger scale-out or scale-in actions in response to C P U, network, or custom metrics. A developer concern is ensuring the instances launched by the ASG are ready to serve traffic — this is why bootstrapping and health checks matter. A common mistake is failing to set correct health checks, which can leave unhealthy instances registered or cause excessive replacement churn. Concrete example: create an ASG with desired capacity 2, min 1, max 4, and target tracking policy to maintain 50% average C P U. If a spike occurs, the ASG launches instances per the launch template; when load drops, it terminates instances to reduce cost. Consider how to make your application stateless so any new instance can join the fleet without manual configuration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Auto Scaling Groups
ASG responsibilities
  • Launch and terminate instances according to capacity settings.
  • Use launch templates to ensure instances are consistent and bootstrapped.
  • Respond to scaling policies tied to CloudWatch metrics or schedules.
Sizing example
Desired: 2 | Min: 1 | Max: 4 — target tracking keeps average CPU at a chosen value.
Concrete advisor
Ensure instances register with the ALB only after successful boot and health checks. Use lifecycle hooks or health checks to avoid sending traffic to partially configured instances.
Common mistake
Not configuring proper health checks leads to unhealthy instances remaining in service and degrading user experience.

screens.title: ASG Scaling Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Auto Scaling provides multiple policy types to control how and when capacity changes occur. Simple scaling performs a single adjustment after a breach of an alarm; step scaling allows you to define multiple adjustments depending on the severity of the metric breach; target tracking adjusts capacity to keep a metric near a target value, for example maintaining 50% average C P U utilization. Target tracking is often the simplest to reason about for developer teams because it behaves like a thermostat: set the target and the ASG attempts to meet it automatically. Step scaling is useful when you want graduated responses to different load levels, and simple scaling can be acceptable for ad-hoc adjustments. A concrete example from the chapter: configure a target tracking policy on average C P U at 50% so the ASG scales out when C P U rises above that level and scales in when it falls. A common misconception is that aggressive scaling prevents any performance impact — improper cooldowns or too-large scaling steps can cause oscillation or overshoot. Always test your scaling policy under realistic load and monitor the ASG activity history to fine tune cooldown and step sizes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › ASG Scaling Policies
Policy types
Simple scaling
One-off adjustment after alarm
Step scaling
Graduated adjustments per breach level
Target tracking
Maintain a metric target like 50% CPU
Target tracking is usually the most maintainable for developers because you express intent, not manual steps. Always set appropriate cooldowns and test under realistic load to avoid thrashing.
Concrete example
Create a target tracking policy to keep average CPU at 50%. When CPU climbs, ASG launches instances; when it drops, ASG terminates instances to save cost.
Pitfall
No cooldown or oversized steps can cause oscillation — tune parameters based on observed behavior.

screens.title: Elastic Load Balancer Types: ALB, NLB, CLB
screens.narratorSegment: Elastic Load Balancing offers ALB, NLB, and the older Classic LB. The Application Load Balancer operates at layer 7 and is ideal for HTTP/HTTPS applications that require host- or path-based routing, header inspection, or redirects. The Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and is optimized for extreme performance, static IPs, and TCP/UDP traffic. Classic Load Balancer is legacy and supports both HTTP and TCP but lacks many advanced features of ALB and NLB. For most web apps, ALB is the default: it routes requests to target groups, performs HTTP health checks, and supports routing rules based on URL paths. A concrete example: use ALB for a microservice architecture that sends /api requests to one target group and /static to another. Use NLB when you need very low latency or preserve the client IP at the connection layer. A common misconception is assuming ALB can handle all protocols with equal efficiency — for raw TCP or UDP workloads, NLB is the correct choice. When in doubt, favor ALB for HTTP workloads and NLB for transport-layer performance requirements. Elastic Load Balancer Types: ALB, NLB, CLB means choose alb for http(s) routing and advanced request features, nlb for raw transport performance, and avoid clb for new architectures.. In practical terms, when to use application, network, or classic load balancers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Load Balancer Types
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Layer 7 routing for HTTP/HTTPS. Use for host/path routing and routing to target groups of EC2, IPs, or Lambda.
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Layer 4, high performance, static IPs. Use for TCP/UDP and very low-latency needs.
Classic Load Balancer (CLB)
Legacy option; supports HTTP and TCP but lacks advanced ALB/NLB features. Avoid for new apps.
Concrete routing example
An ALB routes /api requests to the backend API target group and /assets to a static file target group. The ALB performs health checks and only sends traffic to healthy instances.

screens.title: ALB, Target Groups, and Health Checks
screens.narratorSegment: An ALB routes HTTP(s) traffic to one or more target groups, each of which is a logical set of targets such as EC2 instances, IP addresses, or Lambda functions. The ALB uses health checks configured per target group to determine which targets are healthy and eligible to receive traffic. A typical architecture pairs an ALB with an ASG of EC2 instances: the ASG registers instances with the target group and the ALB only routes to instances that pass the health check path, such as '/'. This protects users from hitting instances that are still booting or failing. A developer example: an ASG launches a new instance that runs user data to install the app; the ALB health check will mark the instance healthy only after the app responds successfully, preventing premature traffic routing. Common mistake: setting overly permissive health checks that don't verify the application layer — for ALB, health checks should exercise an application endpoint to validate readiness. Consider sticky sessions only if absolutely necessary; stateless apps scale more predictably. Reflect: what endpoint will you use for readiness checks that indicates the application is truly ready?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › ALB & Health Checks
Routing and health checks
ALB sends traffic to targets in a target group only when health checks pass. Health checks should exercise a meaningful application endpoint, not just the server port. The ASG registers instances; the ALB performs health checks and routes traffic across Availability Zones for high availability.
Readiness example
Use an endpoint that reflects application readiness, for example '/health/ready' which checks database connectivity and background workers.
Concrete scenario
ASG boots instances from launch template; instance completes user data, application binds to port, responds on '/' and ALB marks it healthy before sending traffic.
Mistake
Using TCP or simple port checks for an HTTP app can cause ALB to mark an unhealthy app as healthy unless the application-level endpoint is validated.

screens.title: Putting It Together: ALB + ASG + EBS
screens.narratorSegment: A common and effective production pattern is an Application Load Balancer in front of an Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances, each using EBS for any necessary persistent storage. In this architecture, the ALB distributes HTTP traffic to the ASG’s instances across multiple Availability Zones. The ASG maintains desired capacity using a launch template that includes user data to install and start the application. If the app requires persistent data, attach EBS volumes or use external state stores; prefer stateless services where possible because state limits elasticity. For backups, snapshot volumes regularly and copy snapshots across regions for disaster recovery. Developer workflows benefit when new instances are bootstrapped with the latest code via CI/CD so scale-out events immediately serve the current release. A concrete walkthrough: create a launch template that installs Nginx and a sample page, create an ALB with a target group and health check, then create an ASG sized desired=2 min=1 max=4 with target tracking at 50% C P U. After launching, access the ALB DNS to see responses from different instance hostnames as traffic is distributed. What parts of this deployment will you automate in your pipeline to ensure repeatable, secure launches?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Integrated Architecture
Pattern summary
ALB routes across AZs to an ASG of EC2 instances. Instances use EBS for data that must persist. Launch templates ensure consistent configuration and user data bootstraps the application automatically.
Deployment checklist
  • Create a launch template with user data to install the app.
  • Create an ALB and a target group with meaningful health checks.
  • Create an ASG attached to the target group with desired/min/max and a target tracking policy.
  • Automate snapshots and ensure cross-region copies if required.
Concrete verify
After creating the ASG and ALB, open the ALB DNS. Refresh to observe different instance hostnames served by the load balancer as traffic is distributed.
Consideration
If your app stores session state locally, either externalize state or carefully consider sticky sessions, which complicate scaling.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create ALB + Launch Template + ASG
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on sequence walks through the practical creation of a launch template, an Application Load Balancer, and an Auto Scaling Group — the exact steps you'll perform in the console. First, create a launch template named 'web-app-template' using an Amazon Linux 2 AMI, t2. micro, a key pair, and a security group allowing SSH and HTTP. Include a user data script that installs Nginx and writes a simple index page. Next, create an ALB named 'my-web-app-alb' in at least two Availability Zones, set a security group allowing HTTP from anywhere, and create a target group 'web-app-tg' with HTTP health check path '/'. Finally, create an ASG named 'my-web-app-asg' using the launch template, attach it to the ALB target group, and set desired capacity 2, min 1, max 4 with a target tracking scaling policy on average C P U at 50. Verification: wait for two instances to launch, confirm they register in the ALB target group, and open the ALB DNS to see the hello page. To test scaling, run a C P U stress on an instance and observe ASG activity triggering new instance launches. This lab reinforces automation, observability, and recovery practices.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Hands-on Activity
Step checklist
  1. Create launch template 'web-app-template' with Amazon Linux 2, t2.micro, key pair, security group.
  2. Add user data to install Nginx and write index page identifying hostname.
  3. Create ALB 'my-web-app-alb' across ≥2 AZs, security group allowing HTTP, create target group 'web-app-tg' with path '/'.
  4. Create ASG 'my-web-app-asg' using the launch template, attach to 'web-app-tg', set desired 2, min 1, max 4, add target tracking at 50% CPU.
Verification steps
  • Wait for 2 instances to launch and register in the ALB target group.
  • Open the ALB DNS name: you should see the Hello page with instance hostnames.
  • Trigger CPU load on an instance and watch ASG activity for scale-out events.
Safety note
Clean up resources after testing to avoid unnecessary costs and revoke broad security group rules when not needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Review the essentials. First, EBS volumes are persistent block storage; pick a volume type that matches IOPS or throughput needs and snapshot regularly for recovery. Second, Auto Scaling Groups automate instance capacity using launch templates and scaling policies; target tracking simplifies scaling behavior. Third, Application Load Balancers route HTTP traffic to target groups and rely on application-level health checks to protect users from unhealthy instances. These three building blocks work together: use launch templates to ensure instances boot with the right software, ASGs to keep capacity aligned with demand, and ALBs to distribute and monitor traffic. Keep applications stateless where possible, avoid embedding secrets in user data, and test snapshot restores and scaling behavior under realistic load. Use this checklist to make sure your EC2-based application is resilient, observable, and automated.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will connect three practical concerns every developer faces in production: durable block storage, automatic compute scaling, and traffic distribution. You will learn how Amazon EBS provides persistent, network-attached block volumes and when to choose SSD or HDD types. We will then build on that storage foundation to explore Auto Scaling Groups, which automatically adjust EC2 capacity using launch templates and scaling policies. Finally, you will see how Elastic Load Balancers route traffic to targets and perform health checks so your application remains available across Availability Zones. Along the way I’ll give concrete examples, like creating a launch template with user data to install Nginx, configuring an Application Load Balancer to route HTTP traffic, and using a target tracking policy to maintain average C P U utilization. We’ll also highlight common pitfalls, such as relying on ephemeral instance store volumes for critical data or forgetting health checks. By the end, you’ll understand the developer implications of integrating EBS, ASG, and ELB and be able to design a highly available, cost-aware architecture that supports CI/CD deployments.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to pick the right EBS volume type for a workload, create and restore EBS snapshots for durable backups, configure Auto Scaling Groups to change EC2 capacity automatically, and set up an Application Load Balancer with target groups and health checks. Each objective is both conceptual and practical: you will differentiate gp3, io2, st1 and sc1 in terms of IOPS and throughput, and you will understand when snapshots are the right recovery mechanism. You will practice creating a launch template that embeds a user data script to bootstrap instances and then link that template to an ASG. Finally, you will configure an ALB routing HTTP traffic to target groups and ensure ALB health checks protect your fleet. These skills matter because they let you build applications that tolerate failures, handle variable load, and minimize manual intervention. To verify competency you will be able to explain why ephemeral instance store volumes are unsuitable for critical data and demonstrate a working ALB + ASG connection using a launch template.

These objectives translate into developer actions you will perform. First, you will pick an EBS type for your workload and justify that choice: for example selecting gp3 for boot and general workloads, io2 for a transactional database that needs provisioned IOPS, and st1 for log processing jobs. Second, you will author a launch template with user data that installs and starts your app so new instances are deployable by CI/CD pipelines. Third, you will create an ALB with a target group and configure health checks that prevent unhealthy instances from receiving traffic. Fourth, you will configure an Auto Scaling Group with a target tracking policy to maintain a chosen C P U utilization and observe scale-out events when load increases. Each objective includes a concrete verification step: deploy a two-instance ASG behind an ALB, hit the ALB DNS to see the sample page, and trigger scaling via a C P U load test. These tasks are practical: they reduce manual toil, enable repeatable deployments, and make your service resilient to failure.

Amazon Elastic Block Store provides persistent block-level storage for EC2 instances. Unlike ephemeral instance store, which is tied to the lifecycle of a single instance and disappears on stop or termination, EBS volumes persist independently. They are network-attached within an Availability Zone and can be detached from one instance and attached to another in the same AZ. This makes EBS suitable for data that must survive instance replacement, such as databases and user data directories. A common example is attaching an EBS volume as a boot volume or separate data volume for a database; if the instance fails, the volume remains and can be reattached after launching a replacement. A frequent misconception is treating EBS as remote object storage: EBS behaves like a block device to the OS, not an object store; snapshots are stored in S3 but an EBS volume itself is presented as a disk. Key operational tips: ensure your data is on EBS for critical state, take snapshots regularly to protect against accidental deletion, and remember EBS volumes are zonal — to move data across regions you must snapshot and copy. When designing for high availability, combine EBS with AMIs and automation so new instances can reattach volumes or restore from snapshots without manual steps. What will you preserve in EBS versus rebuild from code and configuration?

EBS offers several volume types optimized for different input and output profiles. General purpose SSDs, gp2 and gp3, provide a balance of cost and performance and are excellent for boot volumes and development environments. For transactional systems that need high and consistent IOPS, io1 and io2 (Block Express variants) let you provision IOPS separately from size, making them ideal for databases and latency-sensitive workloads. For throughput-oriented tasks, such as big data processing, ETL, or log aggregation, st1 (throughput-optimized HDD) offers cost-effective sequential throughput. sc1 is a cold HDD for infrequent access to large datasets. A concrete decision example: a small web server uses gp3 for boot and app files; a relational database with heavy write activity uses io2 to meet latency and IOPS guarantees; an analytics cluster processing large sequential scans uses st1. A common misconception is assuming SSDs always outperform HDDs; for large sequential reads/writes where throughput matters more than IOPS, st1 can be far more cost-effective. When you plan capacity, document the workload input and output pattern, expected throughput, and cost constraints. Also consider snapshot frequency and restore time when selecting volume type, since the recovery plan affects availability and cost.

EBS snapshots create a point-in-time backup of a volume and are stored incrementally in Amazon S3. The typical process is straightforward: first, quiesce application writes if possible to ensure consistency; second, create a snapshot of the volume; third, snapshots store only changed blocks after the initial full snapshot, which saves storage and time. To recover, you create a new volume from a snapshot and attach it to an instance in the same Availability Zone, or copy the snapshot to another region then create a volume in that region. A concrete example: schedule nightly snapshots for a database volume; if an instance is accidentally terminated, create a new EC2 instance, create a volume from the latest snapshot, attach it, and start the database to restore state. Common misconceptions include treating snapshots as instantaneous full copies — the first snapshot captures all blocks but subsequent snapshots are incremental and the restore process reconstructs the full volume. Operational tips: automate snapshots via lifecycle policies, test restores regularly, and consider snapshot copy to another region for disaster recovery. How will you incorporate snapshot testing into your deployment pipeline?

A launch template encapsulates the configuration an Auto Scaling Group uses to start EC2 instances: AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, and user data for bootstrapping. The user data script is executed on first boot and is an excellent place to install runtime dependencies. For example, the lesson’s sample bootstrap installs and starts Nginx and writes a simple H T M L file identifying the instance by hostname. Concrete example: a user data script that runs on Amazon Linux 2 will update packages, install Nginx, start the service, and create an index page using the instance hostname. Common mistakes include placing secrets directly in user data, which is visible to anyone who can describe the instance; instead use parameter stores or encrypted user data. Also avoid lengthy manual configuration in user data — prefer configuration management or immutable AMIs for repeatable builds. As a verification step, create the launch template, provision an ASG with two instances, and confirm each instance returns the expected H T M L page. How will you keep your bootstrap reproducible and secure across deployments?

An Auto Scaling Group manages a collection of EC2 instances and automatically adjusts capacity to meet defined requirements. It uses a launch template to create new instances with consistent configuration, and it enforces minimum, desired, and maximum capacity so you have predictable bounds on cost and availability. ASGs are typically integrated with CloudWatch metrics and scaling policies, allowing the group to trigger scale-out or scale-in actions in response to C P U, network, or custom metrics. A developer concern is ensuring the instances launched by the ASG are ready to serve traffic — this is why bootstrapping and health checks matter. A common mistake is failing to set correct health checks, which can leave unhealthy instances registered or cause excessive replacement churn. Concrete example: create an ASG with desired capacity 2, min 1, max 4, and target tracking policy to maintain 50% average C P U. If a spike occurs, the ASG launches instances per the launch template; when load drops, it terminates instances to reduce cost. Consider how to make your application stateless so any new instance can join the fleet without manual configuration.

Auto Scaling provides multiple policy types to control how and when capacity changes occur. Simple scaling performs a single adjustment after a breach of an alarm; step scaling allows you to define multiple adjustments depending on the severity of the metric breach; target tracking adjusts capacity to keep a metric near a target value, for example maintaining 50% average C P U utilization. Target tracking is often the simplest to reason about for developer teams because it behaves like a thermostat: set the target and the ASG attempts to meet it automatically. Step scaling is useful when you want graduated responses to different load levels, and simple scaling can be acceptable for ad-hoc adjustments. A concrete example from the chapter: configure a target tracking policy on average C P U at 50% so the ASG scales out when C P U rises above that level and scales in when it falls. A common misconception is that aggressive scaling prevents any performance impact — improper cooldowns or too-large scaling steps can cause oscillation or overshoot. Always test your scaling policy under realistic load and monitor the ASG activity history to fine tune cooldown and step sizes.

Elastic Load Balancing offers ALB, NLB, and the older Classic LB. The Application Load Balancer operates at layer 7 and is ideal for HTTP/HTTPS applications that require host- or path-based routing, header inspection, or redirects. The Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and is optimized for extreme performance, static IPs, and TCP/UDP traffic. Classic Load Balancer is legacy and supports both HTTP and TCP but lacks many advanced features of ALB and NLB. For most web apps, ALB is the default: it routes requests to target groups, performs HTTP health checks, and supports routing rules based on URL paths. A concrete example: use ALB for a microservice architecture that sends /api requests to one target group and /static to another. Use NLB when you need very low latency or preserve the client IP at the connection layer. A common misconception is assuming ALB can handle all protocols with equal efficiency — for raw TCP or UDP workloads, NLB is the correct choice. When in doubt, favor ALB for HTTP workloads and NLB for transport-layer performance requirements. Elastic Load Balancer Types: ALB, NLB, CLB means choose alb for http(s) routing and advanced request features, nlb for raw transport performance, and avoid clb for new architectures..
